abstract: In Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, fibrillar aggregates of the -synuclein (-syn) protein are released into the extracellular space and drive disease progression, yet the mechanisms governing their in vivo neuronal uptake and clearance remain poorly understood. Heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) act as receptors for -syn fibril internalization in iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and could therefore advance synucleinopathy progression in patients. Here we show that -syn fibrils interact electrostatically with the sulfate groups in the HS chains with high affinity, and that genetically reducing the sulfation of neuronal HS reduces the accumulation of -syn aggregates in multiple brain areas, the loss of dopaminergic neurons, and the development of a locomotor behavioral phenotype in mice intracerebrally injected with -syn recombinant fibrils (PFFs). In vivo imaging revealed that HS is also a molecular obstacle to the glymphatic clearance of -syn fibrils, as radiolabeled -syn PFFs travel faster through the brain towards cerebrospinal clearance in mice with less sulfated neuronal HS than in wild-type mice. Collectively, this study provides in vivo evidence that neuronal HS accelerates -syn pathology, potentially by promoting neuronal uptake while slowing the glymphatic clearance of -syn fibrils and, therefore, is a promising therapeutic target to halt synucleinopathies.

summary: Neuronal heparan sulfate sulfation promotes brain uptake and slows glymphatic clearance of α-synuclein fibrils, accelerating synucleinopathy pathology in mice.
